items.question: A dataset contains test scores: 72, 85, 78, 92, 88, 76, 95, 83, 79, 81, 86, 74, 90, 77, 84. Create a dot plot and a histogram (with bins of width 5 starting at 70). Discuss which representation better shows the distribution of scores and why.

rubric.4: Accurate dot plot with each value plotted; histogram with correct bins (70-74, 75-79, 80-84, 85-89, 90-95) and frequencies; thoughtful comparison noting dot plot shows individual values while histogram shows overall shape better for larger datasets
rubric.3: Both representations correct with adequate comparison
rubric.2: Both representations created but comparison weak or one has errors

items.question: The ages of participants in two fitness programs are recorded. Program A: 25, 28, 32, 35, 38, 42, 45, 48, 52, 55. Program B: 22, 24, 26, 28, 30, 58, 62, 65, 68, 72. Part A: Create back-to-back stem plots for both programs. Part B: Describe the shape of each distribution. Part C: Which program has greater variability? Explain.

rubric.4: Correct back-to-back stem plot; A is roughly uniform/symmetric from 20s-50s; B is bimodal with cluster in 20s and 60s; B has greater variability due to spread across both ends with gap in middle
rubric.3: All parts correct with minor errors
rubric.2: Two parts substantially correct

items.question: Company salary data (in thousands): 35, 38, 42, 45, 48, 52, 55, 62, 75, 340. Create a box plot and discuss how the outlier affects the representation. Then explain why a histogram might be misleading and suggest an alternative approach.

rubric.4: Correct box plot identifying 340 as outlier (using 1.5×IQR rule); discusses how outlier stretches scale making other data compressed; suggests using broken axis, log scale, or removing outlier with notation; or presenting summary stats with and without outlier
rubric.3: Correct box plot with adequate discussion of outlier effect and alternative
rubric.2: Box plot correct but weak discussion, or good discussion with plotting errors
rubric.1: Some correct elements but significant errors

items.question: A survey of 200 students shows: 120 play sports, 80 play music, and 40 do both. Part A: Create a two-way frequency table. Part B: What is the probability that a randomly selected student plays sports given that they play music? Part C: Are playing sports and playing music independent events? Show your work.

rubric.4: A: Correct table (Sports&Music:40, Sports only:80, Music only:40, Neither:40); B: P(S|M) = 40/80 = 0.5; C: P(S) = 120/200 = 0.6 ≠ P(S|M) = 0.5, so NOT independent
rubric.3: All parts correct with minor calculation errors
rubric.2: Two parts correct

items.question: Medical test data: 95% of people with a disease test positive (sensitivity). 90% of people without the disease test negative (specificity). If 2% of the population has the disease, and a person tests positive, what is the probability they actually have the disease? Explain why this result might be surprising.

rubric.4: Uses Bayes' theorem or tree diagram: P(D|+) = P(+|D)P(D) / P(+) = (0.95)(0.02) / [(0.95)(0.02) + (0.10)(0.98)] = 0.019 / 0.117 ≈ 0.162 or 16.2%; explains base rate fallacy - low disease prevalence means false positives dominate
rubric.3: Correct calculation with adequate explanation of surprising result
rubric.2: Calculation mostly correct but weak explanation, or vice versa
rubric.1: Attempts but significant errors in probability reasoning

items.question: Data shows that among 500 customers: 300 bought Product A, 250 bought Product B, and 100 bought both. Create a Venn diagram and calculate: the probability a customer bought only A, the probability of buying A or B, and interpret what the overlap tells the marketing team.

rubric.4: Correct Venn: Only A = 200, Only B = 150, Both = 100, Neither = 50; P(only A) = 200/500 = 0.4; P(A or B) = 400/500 = 0.8; interprets: 20% buy both suggesting bundle opportunity, products may be complementary
rubric.3: All calculations correct with reasonable interpretation
rubric.2: Calculations correct but weak interpretation, or minor errors

items.question: Data on study hours (x) and exam scores (y): (2, 65), (3, 72), (4, 78), (5, 82), (6, 88), (7, 91). Part A: Find the least-squares regression line. Part B: Interpret the slope in context. Part C: Predict the score for 8 hours of study. Part D: Explain why predicting for 20 hours might be problematic.

rubric.4: A: y = 5.4x + 54.3 (or equivalent); B: Each additional hour of study is associated with approximately 5.4 more points on the exam; C: y(8) = 5.4(8) + 54.3 = 97.5; D: Extrapolation beyond data range is unreliable; diminishing returns likely, scores capped at 100
rubric.3: All parts correct with minor errors
rubric.2: Three parts substantially correct

items.question: A scatterplot of car age (years) vs. value (thousands of dollars) shows a curved pattern. The data: (1, 28), (2, 24), (3, 20), (4, 17), (5, 14), (7, 10), (10, 6). Explain why a linear model is inappropriate, then find an exponential model of the form y = ab^x and use it to predict the value of an 8-year-old car.

rubric.4: Notes curvature/decreasing rate of change suggests exponential decay; fits model y = 32(0.85)^x or similar; predicts y(8) = 32(0.85)^8 ≈ 8.7 thousand; discusses model fit
rubric.3: Correct model type identification, reasonable exponential fit, correct prediction
rubric.2: Identifies need for exponential but errors in fitting or prediction
rubric.0: No response or uses linear model

items.question: A regression analysis of height (cm) and weight (kg) for adults gives: ŷ = 0.9x - 70, r² = 0.64. Interpret r² in context. If a person's residual is -5 kg, explain what this means. Then discuss whether this relationship implies that gaining height causes weight gain.

rubric.4: r² = 0.64 means 64% of variation in weight is explained by height; residual of -5 kg means person weighs 5 kg less than predicted by their height; relationship is correlation not causation - third variables (genetics, nutrition) affect both
rubric.3: All interpretations correct with minor gaps
rubric.2: Two of three interpretations correct

items.question: A researcher wants to estimate the average commute time for all employees in a large company. Describe how to select a simple random sample of 50 employees. Then explain why convenience sampling (asking the first 50 people in the lobby) could produce biased results.

rubric.4: SRS method: assign each employee a number, use random number generator to select 50; bias in convenience sample: lobby at certain time captures specific shift workers, excludes remote workers, may over-represent early arrivers who may have shorter commutes
rubric.3: Correct SRS method with adequate bias explanation
rubric.2: SRS correct but weak bias explanation, or vice versa

items.question: A school district wants to survey parents about a new policy. Part A: Describe a stratified random sample design using grade levels. Part B: Describe a cluster sample design using schools. Part C: Which design would you recommend if the district wants to ensure representation from each grade level? Explain the trade-offs.

rubric.4: A: Divide parents by child's grade (K, 1, 2,... 12), randomly sample proportionally from each stratum; B: Randomly select several schools, survey all parents at those schools; C: Stratified ensures each grade represented proportionally; trade-offs: stratified more complex but better representation, cluster easier but may miss variation between schools
rubric.3: Both designs correct with reasonable recommendation
rubric.2: Both designs described but weak comparison

items.question: A political poll reports that 52% of voters support Candidate A with a margin of error of ±3%. Explain what the margin of error means, why larger sample sizes reduce it, and why we cannot conclude Candidate A will definitely win.

rubric.4: Margin of error: the interval (49%, 55%) likely contains true population proportion; larger samples reduce sampling variability (MOE ∝ 1/√n); cannot conclude win because 50% is within interval (49-55%), election outcome uncertain
rubric.3: All three components addressed adequately
rubric.2: Two components correct

items.question: A sample of 100 light bulbs has a mean lifespan of 1200 hours with a standard deviation of 100 hours. Construct a 95% confidence interval for the population mean lifespan. Interpret this interval in context.

rubric.4: CI: x̄ ± z*(s/√n) = 1200 ± 1.96(100/10) = 1200 ± 19.6 = (1180.4, 1219.6); interpretation: we are 95% confident the true mean lifespan of all light bulbs is between 1180 and 1220 hours
rubric.3: Correct calculation with adequate interpretation
rubric.2: Calculation correct but weak interpretation, or minor errors

items.question: A simulation generates 1000 bootstrap samples from a dataset. The middle 95% of the sample means range from 45.2 to 52.8. Explain what this bootstrap confidence interval means. Compare this approach to the traditional formula-based method and discuss when each might be preferred.

rubric.4: Bootstrap CI: (45.2, 52.8) gives 95% confidence for population mean based on resampling; traditional uses formula assuming normality; bootstrap preferred when distribution non-normal or formula unavailable; traditional preferred for known distributions and computational simplicity
rubric.3: Correct interpretation with adequate comparison
rubric.2: Interpretation correct but weak comparison, or vice versa

items.question: An engineer claims a new battery lasts more than 500 hours on average. A sample of 36 batteries has mean 515 hours and standard deviation 60 hours. Part A: State null and alternative hypotheses. Part B: Calculate the test statistic. Part C: Find the p-value and make a conclusion at α = 0.05. Part D: Explain Type I and Type II errors in this context.

rubric.4: A: H₀: μ = 500, Hₐ: μ > 500; B: z = (515-500)/(60/6) = 15/10 = 1.5; C: p-value = P(Z > 1.5) ≈ 0.067 > 0.05, fail to reject H₀; D: Type I = concluding battery lasts >500 when it doesn't, Type II = failing to detect improvement when it exists
rubric.3: All parts correct with minor errors
rubric.2: Three parts correct

items.question: A standard deck of 52 cards is used. Event A: drawing a heart. Event B: drawing a face card. Describe the sample space for drawing one card, then find P(A), P(B), P(A and B), and P(A or B). Show whether A and B are independent.

rubric.3: All probabilities correct, independence check correct
rubric.2: Most probabilities correct, minor errors

items.question: At a company, 60% of employees are engineers, 30% are managers, and 10% are support staff. Among engineers, 40% have advanced degrees; among managers, 70% have advanced degrees; among support staff, 10% have advanced degrees. If an employee is selected at random and has an advanced degree, what is the probability they are an engineer?

rubric.3: Correct calculation with minor errors
rubric.2: Correct approach but significant calculation errors
rubric.1: Attempts conditional probability but fundamental errors

items.question: Explain the difference between mutually exclusive events and independent events. Create an example of each using rolling a die, and prove mathematically why one property implies the other cannot hold (for events with non-zero probability).

rubric.4: Mutually exclusive: A∩B = ∅ (e.g., roll 1 and roll 6); Independent: P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) (e.g., two dice, first is even and second is >4); Proof: if mutually exclusive, P(A∩B) = 0, but independent requires P(A)P(B) = 0, impossible if both P(A), P(B) > 0
rubric.3: Correct definitions and examples with adequate proof
rubric.2: Definitions and examples correct but proof incomplete

items.question: A bag contains 5 red balls and 3 blue balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. Part A: Find P(second is red | first is red). Part B: Find P(second is red | first is blue). Part C: Find P(both are red). Part D: Explain why these events are not independent.

rubric.4: A: If first red, 4 red left out of 7, so P = 4/7; B: If first blue, 5 red out of 7, so P = 5/7; C: P(both red) = (5/8)(4/7) = 20/56 = 5/14; D: Not independent because P(2nd red | 1st red) ≠ P(2nd red | 1st blue), i.e., outcome of first affects second
rubric.3: All parts correct with minor errors
rubric.2: Three parts correct

items.question: In a certain city, 20% of days are rainy. On rainy days, 60% of people carry umbrellas. On non-rainy days, 15% of people carry umbrellas. If you see someone with an umbrella, what is the probability it is raining? Construct a tree diagram to solve this problem.

rubric.4: Tree diagram with: Rain (0.2) → Umbrella (0.6) = 0.12, No Rain (0.8) → Umbrella (0.15) = 0.12; P(Umbrella) = 0.12 + 0.12 = 0.24; P(Rain|Umbrella) = 0.12/0.24 = 0.5
rubric.3: Correct calculation with tree diagram, minor errors
rubric.2: Tree diagram correct but calculation errors, or correct answer without diagram

items.question: A diagnostic test for a rare disease affects 1 in 10,000 people has 99% sensitivity (correctly identifies those with disease) and 98% specificity (correctly identifies those without disease). A person tests positive. Calculate the probability they actually have the disease, and explain why false positive rate matters for rare conditions.

rubric.4: P(D|+) = P(+|D)P(D) / [P(+|D)P(D) + P(+|D')P(D')] = (0.99)(0.0001) / [(0.99)(0.0001) + (0.02)(0.9999)] = 0.000099 / 0.020097 ≈ 0.0049 or about 0.5%; explains base rate fallacy: even with high specificity, the 2% false positive rate applied to 9,999 healthy people produces ~200 false positives, dwarfing the ~1 true positive
rubric.3: Correct calculation with adequate explanation
rubric.2: Calculation mostly correct with weak explanation
